answer: When the same file changed in two places, sync did not merge or keep the newer write. It wrote a **conflicting copy** and notified the user, who then cleaned up the duplicates by hand. The memory doesn't mention 2022 or say why last-write-wins was rejected. It does say sync reconciles whole files rather than character-level diffs, and that CRDT-style merging was considered too immature and complex, with attempts removed because of too many edge cases. Keeping conflict copies is also described as simple and hard to corrupt.
block:
--- ADR/002 Sync Engine.md ---
Context | Consequences > Negative / trade-offs
* **No real-time collaboration.** Two people editing one file at once get a conflicting copy, not a live merged document.
* **Conflict copies need manual cleanup.** The user resolves the duplicates by hand.
* **Polling latency.** Changes propagate on a ~5–20s cycle, not instantly.

--- ADR/007 Core Application Logic on the Client.md ---
Context | Consequences > Negative / trade-offs
* **Every client builds and holds its own copy.** Each browser/device must sync all files locally and (re)create its own [[Object Index|object index]] from scratch — duplicated storage and a cold-start indexing cost on every new client, instead of indexing once on the server. Partly mitigated by selective sync (e.g. [[Document|documents]] are fetched on demand) — see [[Sync]].
* **No thin-client / server-only option.** Large spaces or constrained, low-power devices that could previously lean on server mode no longer can — there is no mode where the heavy lifting stays on the server.
* **Server-authoritative features are harder.** Anything needing a central source of truth at edit time — notably real-time collaboration / CRDT merging — does not fall out naturally. Concurrent edits are resolved by writing a conflicting copy rather than merging. See [[ADR/002 Sync Engine]].

--- ADR/002 Sync Engine.md ---
Context | Decision
Sync is **file-level, bidirectional, and poll-based**, running in the service worker (see [[Sync]]):

* the whole space syncs roughly every 20 seconds, the currently open file every 4–5 seconds.
* it reconciles **whole files** by comparing local and remote state, not character-level diffs.
* on a **conflict** (the same file changed in two places) it does **not merge** — it writes a **conflicting copy** and notifies you.

At the time of this decision, more more modern approaches like CRDTs were not yet very mature and integrating them was deemed too complex. At various stages such integration was attempted, but later removed because of too many edge cases.

--- ADR/002 Sync Engine.md ---
Context | Consequences > Positive
* **Simple.** Whole-file sync with conflict-copies is easy to reason about and hard to corrupt.
* **Keeps the server dumb.** File-level sync needs only list/read/write/delete, so the server stays a thin file store ([[ADR/010 Rust Backend]]) and the runtime stays swappable.
 * **Offline-friendly.** Edits made offline reconcile on the next poll without a central coordinator.

--- API/sbShare.md ---
Configuration
Only sync writes are conditional (they pass `{conditional = true}` to `net.writeURI`): they send the ETag of the last read as `If-Match`, so a change made in the meantime makes the write return `{conflict = true}` and sync retries. Push writes never send `If-Match`: the local page replaces the remote one.
